what_its_for: Inebilizumab-Cdon is used to treat adults with a condition called neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD). This is a disease where your immune system mistakenly attacks your spinal cord and optic nerves (the nerves connected to your eyes), which can cause vision loss, weakness, or paralysis. This medicine helps reduce attacks of this disease in people who have a specific antibody in their blood called AQP4-IgG (also called aquaporin-4 antibody positive).
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it is slowly delivered into a vein through a needle. You will NOT give this to yourself at home. A doctor, nurse, or trained healthcare provider will give you this infusion at a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. Each infusion takes about 1.5 hours. Before your infusion, your healthcare team will give you pre-medications (such as a steroid, antihistamine, and fever reducer) to help reduce the risk of infusion reactions. You will be watched closely during and after your infusion for any reactions.
dosing: The usual dosing schedule is: First, you receive two starting doses given 2 weeks apart (called the induction doses). After that, you receive one infusion every 6 months (called the maintenance doses). Your doctor will decide the exact dose based on your medical condition. Do not skip or delay your infusions without talking to your doctor first, as this could increase your risk of a disease attack.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule an infusion appointment, call your doctor or infusion center right away. Do not wait until your next scheduled appointment. Your doctor will work with you to reschedule as soon as possible. Missing doses may increase your risk of having an NMOSD attack, so it is very important to stay on schedule.
storage: This medicine is prepared and stored by healthcare professionals at the clinic or infusion center. You do not need to store it at home. The prepared infusion solution should be kept at room temperature and used within a certain number of hours after preparation. Your healthcare team will handle all storage requirements.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as MMR, chickenpox, shingles Zostavax, nasal flu spray, or yellow fever vaccines) while taking this medicine and for a period after stopping, because this drug weakens part of your immune system and live vaccines could cause serious infections. Talk to your doctor about all vaccines before starting treatment. Try to avoid close contact with people who are sick, especially those with serious infections. Tell your doctor right away if you feel any signs of infection. Do not start this medicine if you currently have an active infection.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor immediately or go to the nearest emergency room if you experience any of the following: signs of a serious allergic or infusion reaction such as trouble breathing, chest tightness, fast heartbeat, dizziness, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or feeling faint; signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, cough, painful urination, or skin sores that do not heal; signs of a nervous system problem such as confusion, memory loss, weakness, or vision changes that could suggest a rare but serious brain infection called PML (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy); new or worsening symptoms of your NMOSD such as sudden vision changes, weakness, or numbness; or any unusual symptoms that concern you. Also tell your doctor if you become pregnant or plan to become pregnant while on this medicine.
when_it_works: This medicine does not cure NMOSD, but it helps prevent future attacks (relapses). You may not feel different right away, but the medicine is working to protect your nerves by reducing harmful immune cells in your body. Most people begin to see a reduction in attacks after starting treatment. It is important to keep all your infusion appointments even if you feel well, because the medicine needs to stay at a steady level in your body to keep protecting you.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine may harm an unborn baby. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before starting this medicine. You should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after your last dose. Children: This medicine is currently approved only for adults. It has not been studied enough in children under 18. Older adults: Older patients can use this medicine, but your doctor will monitor you closely. Liver or kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have any liver or kidney issues, as this may affect how your body handles the medicine. Vaccination: Make sure all of your vaccines are up to date at least 4 weeks before starting this medicine. Talk to your doctor about a plan for any vaccines you may need in the future.
